questions.question: The Mars Climate Orbiter, an American spacecraft, reached Mars in September 1999, flew far too low into the planet's air and was lost. Engineers at the company that built it had sent the mission's navigators figures for every small thruster firing. What did the review board find wrong with those figures?
questions.answer: They were in English units, not metric
choices: They were in English units, not metric
They were rounded off far too roughly
They had two digits swapped by mistake
They came from a faulty thruster sensor
questions.context: The builders' software gave each thruster's push in pound-force seconds, an English unit, while the navigators' software expected newton-seconds, the metric unit, so the craft's path was worked out wrong and it passed only about 57 kilometres above Mars. Mix-ups like this are why scientists everywhere share one system of units, the International System (SI), the modern metric system.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.1E has 6th graders collect quantitative data in SI units, and the lost Mars orbiter is the well-known case of why everyone must share one system.

questions.question: A geologist checks the mass of a bag of rock samples on her field scale, which reads in kilograms. The kilogram is the base unit of mass in the system scientists everywhere use. How many grams make one kilogram?
choices: A thousand grams
A hundred grams
Ten thousand grams
A million grams
questions.context: The prefix kilo-, from the Greek word for a thousand, means a thousand of whatever unit it is put on, so a kilogram is 1,000 grams and a kilometre is 1,000 metres. A hundred of a unit takes the prefix hecto-, a million takes mega-, and ten thousand grams make ten kilograms.
questions.grade_note: Metric prefixes are learned with the SI units 6th graders measure in (TEKS 6.1E), and kilo- on the kilogram, the base unit of mass, is the first of them.

questions.question: A lab worker draws 5 millilitres of blue dye into a syringe, ready to add to a test tube. What part of a litre is one millilitre?
choices: A thousandth of a litre
A millionth of a litre
A hundredth of a litre
A tenth of a litre
questions.context: The prefix milli- comes from the Latin word mille, a thousand, and means a thousandth: 1,000 millilitres fill a litre, just as 1,000 millimetres make a metre. Milli- sounds like million, but a millionth takes the prefix micro-, and a hundredth takes centi-.
questions.grade_note: Milli- is among the metric prefixes 6th graders learn with SI units (TEKS 6.1E), and its likeness to the word million is the mix-up to clear.

questions.question: A botanist measures a leaf with a ruler marked off in units that are each a hundredth of a metre long. What are those units called?
choices: Centimetres
Millimetres
Decimetres
Hectometres
questions.context: The prefix centi-, from the Latin word centum, a hundred, means a hundredth, so 100 centimetres make a metre. A millimetre is a thousandth of a metre and a decimetre a tenth, while a hectometre is not small at all: it is 100 metres.
questions.grade_note: Centi- is among the metric prefixes 6th graders learn with SI units (TEKS 6.1E); naming the hundredth of a metre tests the prefix's meaning, set against its look-alikes.

questions.question: A biologist kneels beside a pond and writes in her field notebook that the water is cloudy and green and smells of rotten eggs. What has she recorded?
choices: Qualitative data
Quantitative data
An inference
A prediction
questions.context: Qualitative data are descriptions in words, such as colour, smell or texture, while quantitative data are measurements in numbers, such as the water's temperature in degrees Celsius; both count as evidence. Her note records what she saw and smelled, not a conclusion drawn from it (an inference) or a guess about what will happen (a prediction).
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.1E asks 6th graders to collect quantitative data in SI units and qualitative data as evidence, so telling the two apart is taught directly.

questions.question: A student rolls a toy car down the same ramp five times and measures how far it travels across the floor. Four runs reach between 118 and 121 centimetres, but one stops at 64 centimetres. What should she do about that short run?
questions.answer: Look for a cause, then run that trial again
choices: Look for a cause, then run that trial again
Erase it from her notes, as it spoils the pattern
Report 64 centimetres as the car's true distance
Decide that the four longer runs were wrong
questions.context: A result far from the rest, called an outlier, may be a fluke or a slip, such as a misread tape measure or a car that clipped a chair leg, so she looks for the cause and repeats that trial. She keeps the odd result in her notes and says what she did with it, because quietly dropping data misleads. One odd run cannot overturn four that agree, and it is not the true distance either.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.1F builds data from repeated trials and 6.2B asks for sources of error, so spotting and rechecking an odd result is 6th-grade practice.

questions.question: Two groups take turns timing the same pendulum through ten swings, and each group runs five trials. One group's times all lie within a fifth of a second of one another, while the other group's are spread across three seconds. Which group's result can the class trust more?
questions.answer: The group whose times agree closely
choices: The group whose times agree closely
The group whose times cover a wider range
Either group, as each one ran five trials
Neither group, as both groups' times vary
questions.context: Trials of the same measurement should agree, and when they do, the result can be trusted to come out the same again. A wide spread shows that something changed from trial to trial, such as slips in starting and stopping the stopwatch, so that group's result is less sure and the group should find the cause and run more trials. A little spread is normal, and close agreement is still no proof of a right answer, since a faulty tool can be off by the same amount every time.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.2B has 6th graders identify the descriptive features of data, and the spread of repeated trials is the one that says how far a result can be trusted.

questions.question: A class measures how much water evaporates in a week from four matching dishes set side by side on a sunny windowsill. One dish has a hairline crack, and water slowly seeps out through it. When the class measures the water left in that dish, what will its result seem to show?
choices: More evaporation than really happened
Less evaporation than really happened
No evaporation at all during the week
Just the same evaporation as the others
questions.context: The class works out evaporation from the water each dish has lost, and the water that seeps through the crack is lost too, so that dish seems to have lost more to evaporation than it really did. A leaky container is a source of error, and a scientist says which way it throws a result off before setting that result aside.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.2B asks 6th graders to identify sources of error, and saying which way a leak throws off a result is the simple why.

questions.question: A student drops a steel ball from a shelf 2 metres up and times each fall with a stopwatch. She makes ten drops from the same spot, and her ten times are all a little different. What causes most of the difference between them?
questions.answer: Her reactions as she starts and stops the watch
choices: Her reactions as she starts and stops the watch
The pull of gravity, which changes between drops
The ball, which falls faster on some drops
The stopwatch's clock, which runs fast, then slow
questions.context: Timing by hand carries the timer's reaction at the start and at the stop, typically about a fifth of a second, and the delay is a little different every time. A ball dropped the same way from the same spot falls in the same time, because gravity's pull at one place holds steady, and a quartz stopwatch drifts only seconds in a month. That is why hand-timed trials are repeated, and why races are now timed electronically.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 6.2B asks for sources of error, and the timer's own reactions are the usual one in the hand-timed labs of 6th grade.
